title: Out loud for others (2:5)
hookLine: it's praiseworthy to admit wrongs against others openly
tomorrow: does a holy day clear a wrong you never fixed?

lines: ROASTED IN PUBLIC, SORRY IN PRIVATE.
IN YOUR HEAD. A WHISPER. ALOUD.
cards: The roast happened in the group chat, with everyone watching. The apology arrived later, by private message. Is a private sorry enough when others heard the wrong?
Here's a small test with your own ears. Say a hard sentence in your head: I was wrong. Easy.
Now say it in a whisper. Now at speaking volume, in a room. The words don't change, but the sound does something to them.
Maimonides knew that, and he cares about the volume.

teach.b: In chapter two he writes that it is very praiseworthy for a returner to confess in public, to make known the wrongs done between them and another person: I wronged so-and-so, I did this, and now I'm turning.
Whoever hides those wrongs out of pride, he says, hasn't finished returning, and he cites Proverbs: "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper." Then comes the twist.
Another verse, in the Psalms, seems to say the opposite: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered."
Covering fails, covering is blessed. Which is it? Maimonides sorts them by who was wronged.
Wrongs against another person are spoken openly, because other people heard them, saw them, carried them. Wrongs between a person and God alone are not broadcast.
There, he says, revealing them would be brazen; that confession is made before God, specifically, and kept covered.
If the wrong had an audience, the admission gets one too.
If it never left the room, it stays there. And the sound itself is part of it.
Hearing your own voice say I did this, to you, out loud, makes it hard to keep the wrong a private matter you've quietly settled with yourself.

how: On Yom Kippur the vidui, the confession, is said aloud together by the congregation in the plural, 'we have sinned'; wrongs against particular people are, by Maimonides' rule, admitted to those people.

games.q: what does “out loud for others” mean?
o: reading the Torah aloud to the whole community
praying aloud so the congregation can follow
admitting wrongs against people where others hear

games.q: which verse, which wrong — tap the pairs.
p: he that covereth his sins shall not prosper
blessed is he whose sin is covered
a wrong between you and God

s: a private apology settles a wrong that others witnessed
Maimonides calls it very praiseworthy to admit wrongs against people openly; hiding them out of pride leaves return unfinished.
Maimonides says every wrong should be confessed in public
wrongs between a person and God alone are not broadcast; revealing them, he says, is brazen.
Maimonides squares two verses that seem to clash, one on covering and one on revealing
Proverbs for wrongs against people, Psalms for wrongs between a person and God.

games.q: you snapped at a teammate during practice, in front of the whole squad. you've already apologized by text. the next practice starts. what does Maimonides' rule point to?
o: say it where it happened: a short word in front of the squad that you were wrong.
nothing more; the text settled it, and bringing it up again reopens it.
keep it covered, like the psalm says; blessed is the one whose sin is covered.
games.why: the wrong had an audience, so the admission gets one. the psalm's covering is for wrongs between a person and God alone.

practice: Choose one person you owe an admission. Quietly, at real speaking volume, say the sentence you'd say to them: their name, what you did, and that you're turning. Then let the room go silent and listen to how it sounded.

wordCard.voice: Out loud for others: Maimonides' rule that wrongs between people are admitted openly, while wrongs between a person and God stay covered.

orig.note: Hebrew: confession, the spoken admission that is part of return.

carryVoice: Your line: admit it to them. Where the wrong was heard, the turning should be heard too. Day fifteen forty-four, said aloud.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:5 (public confession of wrongs between people; wrongs between a person and God not revealed)
